# Sharing skills across a teaching team

Once a task works well in one module, write it down as a skill (chapter 12) and share it. A department then needs each procedure to be worked out only once for all its lecturers.

**Items to share.**

| Item | What it is | Who benefits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Module template | The empty folder layout and a skeleton instruction file (chapter 3) | Anyone starting or inheriting a module |
| Skills | Step-by-step instructions for a recurring task: new lecture, new problem set, annual update, stress test | Colleagues doing the same task |
| Checker | The independent checker from chapter 9, as a stored definition | Lecturers and teaching assistants |
| Statement template | The student-facing AI statement (chapter 11) | The whole programme |

Chapter 12 covers how to write and test a skill. Before sharing one, run its test cases on a module other than the one it was written for.

**Personal, module and department skills.** Personal skills record how you work, such as your written standard below. Module skills hold the procedures for one module and live in its folder, so they pass to whoever teaches it next. Department skills hold what every module should do the same way: the checker, the stress test, the notebook release. Give department skills a common prefix so that they cannot be confused with a module's own, and give each one an owner who reviews changes before they are shared.

**Building a written standard for the reviewer.** The third review pass in chapter 9 needs a document that says how your material should be written. It is built from your own work.

1. **Collect examples.** Five to ten pieces you consider your best: lecture notes, slides, problem sets, or papers if the standard is for research writing.
2. **Have the agent extract the rules.** Ask it to read them and list what is consistent: sentence and paragraph length, how a slide is structured, how a result is introduced, how equations are referenced, what is never done.
3. **Edit the rules yourself.** Delete what is accidental, correct what it misread, and add the rules you know you follow that the examples did not show.
4. **Add pairs of examples.** For each important rule, one passage that breaks it and the corrected version. The pair gives the reviewer something concrete to match.
5. **Add a list of what to flag.** The phrases and constructions you do not want, including those typical of machine-written text.
6. **Say how to report.** Findings as a list with location, the rule broken and a suggested fix. No rewriting.
7. **Test it on old material.** Run the reviewer on something you wrote before the standard existed, and on something an agent wrote. Adjust rules that produce false alarms.
8. **Keep it current.** Each time you correct the agent's writing by hand, ask whether the correction is a rule. If so, add it.

One to three pages is enough. A standard built this way is specific to its author, so share the method and the template with colleagues rather than your own rules. A skeleton is [template G](templates.qmd#tpl-g).

**Where to keep shared files.** Keep them in a departmental repository (chapter 4) or shared drive, with one owner per file, and keep that location free of student data and of assessment content: skills and templates only.

**Teaching assistants.** Give assistants the checker and the problem-set skill but not the assessment folder. Agree in advance what they may use an agent for, and apply the same rule to all assistants on a module.

**Handing a module over.** The instruction file with its decisions log, the figure and solution scripts, and the module's skills together are the handover. A successor can ask the agent to explain how any week's material was built and regenerate it.

> **In Claude Code.** Module skills are committed with the module folder in `.claude/skills/`, and personal skills sit in `~/.claude/skills/` (chapter 12). The checker is a subagent definition in `.claude/agents/`. A department can package its skills and subagents as a [plugin](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins) and list it in a marketplace, which is a Git repository containing a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` file. Colleagues add the marketplace with `claude plugin marketplace add` and install from it with `claude plugin install`. A plugin's skills are called as `/plugin-name:skill-name`, so they cannot clash with a module's own skills.
>
> The documentation warns that an installed plugin can run arbitrary code with your user privileges, and advises reviewing a plugin before installing it, whichever marketplace it comes from ([plugin security](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/security)). Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, so the same files are usable in other tools that support it.
